common_name: Lord Baltimore Hardy Hibiscus (Classic Dinner-Plate Crimson-Red Perennial)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Lord Baltimore is a classic 1955 hybrid hardy hibiscus, still one of the most widely grown red-flowered selections, producing enormous ruffled crimson blooms on a large, sturdy plant.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer since this wetland-edge native hibiscus wilts quickly in dry conditions. Lord Baltimore is a landmark 1955 hybrid, bred from a mix of native swamp and rose mallow hibiscus species, and remains a garden standard decades later for its huge, ruffled, crimson-red flowers that can reach up to 10 inches across, blooming from midsummer into fall on a robust, well-branched plant. Like other hardy hibiscus, it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location and be patient rather than assuming it has died. It is generally pest-free and undemanding given consistently moist, fertile soil, rewarding minimal care with a spectacular tropical-looking summer display from a fully cold-hardy perennial.

common_name: Fireball Hardy Hibiscus (Purple-Foliage Velvety Red-Flowered Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Fireball is a patented hardy hibiscus selection from a 40-year Fleming breeding program, notable for dark purple, maple-like foliage that provides striking contrast to its velvety red flowers all season, not just at bloom time.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer since hardy hibiscus wilts quickly in dry conditions. Fireball stands apart from most hardy hibiscus cultivars for its dark purple, deeply lobed, maple-like foliage, which provides season-long color contrast rather than the plain green leaves typical of the genus, and the compact plant produces velvety red, 10-inch flowers from midsummer into fall. Like other hardy hibiscus it dies back completely to the ground each winter and emerges quite late in spring, so mark its location and be patient rather than assuming it has died. The striking foliage makes it valuable as a bold accent even between bloom flushes, and it is generally pest-free and undemanding given consistently moist, fertile soil.

common_name: Toucan Scarlet Canna (Compact Heat and Humidity-Tolerant Series)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes or vegetatively-propagated transplants once soil has warmed; Toucan Scarlet is a Proven Winners canna series bred for a compact, uniform habit and strong heat and humidity tolerance, well suited to container plantings and Gulf Coast beds.

directions: Plant rhizomes or transplants a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun. Toucan Scarlet is part of a compact, uniform Proven Winners canna series bred for strong performance in both containers and landscape beds, producing vivid scarlet-red blooms above lush, tropical-textured green foliage from early summer through frost. Its more compact size than heirloom canna varieties makes it easier to place in a mixed border or large pot without overwhelming neighboring plants. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.

common_name: Luna Pink Swirl Hibiscus (Compact Picotee-Patterned Hardy Hibiscus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8 weeks before the last frost or set out container plants in spring in moist, fertile soil in full sun; Luna Pink Swirl is part of the compact Luna series, bred for garden and container use, staying well under half the height of older hardy hibiscus varieties.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile soil in full sun, watering deeply and often through summer to keep this wetland-edge native from wilting in hot weather. Luna Pink Swirl bears distinctive picotee-patterned flowers, a swirled blend of pink shades radiating from a dark red center, on the same compact, well-branched, 24-30 inch frame that defines the Luna series, resisting the flopping common in taller hardy hibiscus. It flowers continuously from mid to late summer into fall, providing bold, tropical-looking color from an entirely cold-hardy perennial that dies back to the crown each winter and returns reliably each spring. Cut the dead stalks back to a few inches above ground in late winter, and note that new growth emerges late in spring, so avoid mistaking a dormant crown for a dead plant.
